title: systemd Timers — The Modern Alternative to Cron
lead: Schedule the work; the system runs it for you. You will write a service and a timer, verify the time expression, watch the run with journalctl and compare it with cron.
objectives: You write a `.service` file (`Type=oneshot`, `ExecStart`) and a `.timer` file (`OnCalendar`, `Persistent=true`).
You verify a time expression with `systemd-analyze calendar` before it ever runs.
You install and monitor a timer with `daemon-reload`, `enable --now`, `list-timers` and `journalctl -u`.
You read a cron line (`30 2 * * *`) and write the equivalent timer.
You know user timers (`systemctl --user`) and how to decide between cron and a timer.

sections.title: Why timers? Comparison with cron
body: Running a script by hand is easy; real automation means running it **at the right time**. The classic way is **cron**: five time fields and a command on one line. The modern way is a **systemd timer**: two files, one saying **what** runs (`backup.service`), the other **when** it runs (`backup.timer`).

A cron line: `30 2 * * * /home/student/bin/backup.sh` = every day at 02:30. Fields: minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week. The timer's advantages: output goes to the **journal** (`journalctl -u`), `Persistent=true` catches up a missed run at boot, `RandomizedDelaySec` spreads load, and `systemctl list-timers` shows the next run.
In this module you write the files in the simulator and check their content; `systemctl` and `journalctl` only work on a real VM. Cron's advantage is simplicity: one line, available everywhere.

commands.what: Opens your own cron table in an editor.
commands.where: For simple one-line scheduled jobs.
commands.why: The reference point: you recognise the old job before moving it to a timer.

commands.what: Lists the current cron lines.
commands.where: When taking inventory of jobs to migrate.
commands.why: You see which jobs to convert to timers.

commands.what: Writes a cron line to a file: `minute hour day month weekday command`.
commands.where: To practise cron syntax and keep it in a file.
commands.why: You get used to the right field order.

commands.what: Lists active timers with their next and last run times.
commands.where: When verifying a timer is really scheduled.
commands.why: You catch a silently idle timer immediately.

sections.tip: For a simple one-off user job, cron is enough. Choose a timer when you want logs, dependencies, catch-up and monitoring.

sections.title: The service unit: what runs?
body: The service file defines the command. For scheduled jobs use **`Type=oneshot`**: the command runs and finishes. `ExecStart` requires an **absolute path**; write `/usr/local/bin/backup.sh`, not `backup.sh`.

System units go to `/etc/systemd/system/` (root needed). You cannot write there in the simulator; use the `~/units/` folder instead, the content to copy is identical. Make the script executable first: `chmod +x`.
Note: a `.service` does not need an `[Install]` section; scheduling belongs to the timer. To test by hand, `sudo systemctl start backup.service` is enough.

commands.what: Writes the service unit line by line.
commands.where: In `~/units/` in the sim, under `/etc/systemd/system/` on the VM.
commands.why: You create the file reproducibly without opening an editor.

commands.what: Shows the content of the file you wrote.
commands.where: After every write.
commands.why: You spot typos (`Type=oneshot`, path) before starting.

commands.what: Gives the script execute permission.
commands.where: For every script called by `ExecStart`.
commands.why: Without it the service fails with `203/EXEC`.

commands.what: Checks the unit file's syntax and paths.
commands.where: Before `daemon-reload`.
commands.why: Catches a wrong path or typo without running anything.

sections.tip: Run the unit once by hand with `sudo systemctl start backup.service`; if it works, scheduling it is safe.
sections.warn: On RHEL/Rocky (SELinux) a service may be unable to run a script under `/home` (`203/EXEC`, `Permission denied`). Put the script in `/usr/local/bin`; on Debian/Ubuntu (AppArmor) this is rarer, but the same path is recommended.

sections.title: The timer unit: when does it run?
body: A timer file contains the time in `[Timer]` and the line `WantedBy=timers.target` in `[Install]`. The name matches the service: `backup.timer` → `backup.service`.

**`OnCalendar=`** is calendar time: `*-*-* 02:30:00` every day at 02:30, `Mon *-*-* 08:00:00` every Monday at 08:00; `hourly`, `daily`, `weekly` are shortcuts. **`OnBootSec=`** waits after boot, **`OnUnitActiveSec=`** after the last run.

**`Persistent=true`**: a run missed while the machine was off happens right at the next boot. **`RandomizedDelaySec=`** delays the start randomly, so many machines do not hit a shared resource at once.

commands.what: Defines calendar-based time.
commands.where: For jobs at fixed times such as nightly or weekly.
commands.why: It is the readable counterpart of cron's five fields.

commands.what: Waits a relative time after boot or after the last run.
commands.where: For jobs like "10 min after boot, then every hour".
commands.why: Solves interval-based jobs that have no calendar.

commands.what: Catches up a missed run at the next boot.
commands.where: On laptops, VMs or machines switched off at night.
commands.why: Gives anacron-like safety, which cron lacks.

commands.what: Adds a random delay to the start.
commands.where: On many servers running at the same time.
commands.why: Prevents sudden load spikes on a shared repository or network.

commands.what: Interprets a time expression and shows the next elapse.
commands.where: Before and after writing a timer.
commands.why: A wrong expression silently never runs; here you see it at once.

sections.tip: Lists like `Mon,Fri *-*-* 08:00` and `*-*-* *:00/15:00` (every 15 min) work; test them all with `systemd-analyze calendar` first.

sections.title: Install, start, monitor
body: The order is fixed: write the files → `systemd-analyze verify` and `calendar` → `sudo systemctl daemon-reload` → `start` the service by hand and check `journalctl` → `enable --now` the **timer** → verify with `list-timers`.
`enable --now` applies to the **timer** (`backup.timer`), not the service. If you forget `daemon-reload` after a new or changed file, systemd keeps using the old state.
Read the output with `journalctl -u backup.service`; `-f` follows live, `--since today` filters the day. A failed run shows a `Failed with result` line.

commands.what: Makes systemd re-read the unit files.
commands.where: After every new or changed .service and .timer.
commands.why: Without it systemd sees an old file or none at all.

commands.what: Runs the service once, right now.
commands.where: To test the job itself before enabling the timer.
commands.why: You find errors without waiting for the timer.

commands.what: Enables the timer at boot and starts it immediately.
commands.where: For every permanent timer.
commands.why: It also runs after a reboot.

commands.what: Shows the next and last runs.
commands.where: After installing and when troubleshooting.
commands.why: The NEXT column proves the timer is really scheduled.

commands.what: Shows the log entries of a unit.
commands.where: When reading successful and failed runs.
commands.why: One searchable record instead of cron's mailbox.

sections.warn: A service running as root can do great harm with a script that deletes or moves files. Dry-run the script with `echo` first, verify the path, then schedule it. A wrong `OnCalendar` gives no error; it simply never runs.
sections.danger: Over SSH never stop or disable `sshd` or network services with `systemctl`; you lock yourself out. Experiment only with your own units and take a VM snapshot before important changes (Module 0.2).

sections.title: User timers and the migration decision
body: You can schedule without root: **user units** live in `~/.config/systemd/user/` and are managed with `systemctl --user` (no `sudo`). They stop when you log out; to keep them running use `loginctl enable-linger student`.

Decision: one-line job, output irrelevant → **cron**. Need logs, dependencies (run when the network is up), catch-up (`Persistent`), random delay or resource limits → **timer**. Both can coexist; when migrating, comment out the old cron line, verify the new timer, then delete.
On Debian/Ubuntu packages often ship timers instead of cron (`apt-daily.timer`); on RHEL/Rocky something like `dnf-makecache.timer`. `systemctl list-timers --all` is full of ready examples.

commands.what: Creates the user units folder.
commands.where: Before your first user timer.
commands.why: systemd looks for user units here.

commands.what: Makes systemd re-read user units.
commands.where: After writing the user files.
commands.why: You follow the same flow without `sudo`.

commands.what: Enables and starts a user timer.
commands.where: For personal jobs in your own home.
commands.why: No root needed, so the risk is small.

commands.what: Keeps user units running while you are logged out.
commands.where: On a server where a user timer must continue in the background.
commands.why: Otherwise the timer stops when you log out.

sections.tip: A user timer is the safest place to experiment: if you make a mistake only your own account is affected, not the system.

t01.text: Create the folders `~/bin` and `~/units` with one command: `mkdir -p ~/bin ~/units`.

t02.text: Read the cron sample file: `cat ~/sample/crontab.txt`. It has three job lines.
t02.hint: Lines are: minute hour day month weekday command.

t03.text: Write `~/bin/backup.sh` with `printf`: first line `#!/bin/bash`, second line `echo backup done`.

t05.hint: Separate lines with `\n` in one `printf` and end with `> ~/units/backup.service`.

t06.hint: Use single quotes in the sim so the shell does not expand `*`.

t07.text: Predict: how many lines in `~/sample/list-timers.txt` contain `timer`? Then verify with `grep -c timer ~/sample/list-timers.txt`.
t07.hint: The header has no lowercase `timer`; there are two timer lines.

t08.text: Predict: which time does the `Next elapse` line in `~/sample/analyze.txt` show? Look with `grep 'Next elapse' ~/sample/analyze.txt`.
t08.hint: The expression was Monday 08:00; find the next Monday.

t09.text: Debug: `~/broken/broken.timer` does not work. It has a typo `OnCalender` and the `[Install]` section is missing. Rewrite the file with `OnCalendar=daily`, `Persistent=true` and `WantedBy=timers.target`.

t10.text: Debug: `ExecStart=report.sh` in `~/broken/report.service` is a relative path; systemd rejects it. Rewrite the file so it contains `ExecStart=/home/student/bin/report.sh` (keep `Type=oneshot`).
t10.hint: See the current lines with `cat`, then `printf ... > ~/broken/report.service`.

t11.text: Mini project (user timer): create the folder `~/.config/systemd/user`. `notes.service` must contain `ExecStart=/usr/bin/touch /home/student/notes.txt`; `notes.timer` must contain `OnCalendar=hourly` and `WantedBy=timers.target`.
t11.hint: Three commands: `mkdir -p`, one `printf` for the service, one for the timer.

t12.text: Mini project (cron comparison): write two cron lines to `~/units/backup.cron`: `30 2 * * * /home/student/bin/backup.sh` and `0 8 * * 1 /home/student/bin/report.sh`.
t12.hint: Use `>` for the first line and `>>` for the second.

t13.text: Challenge: for a `cleanup` job write `~/units/cleanup.service` (`ExecStart=/home/student/bin/cleanup.sh`, `Type=oneshot`) and `~/units/cleanup.timer`. Timer: 10 minutes after boot (`OnBootSec=10min`), then every hour (`OnUnitActiveSec=1h`), random delay up to 5 minutes (`RandomizedDelaySec=5min`), `WantedBy=timers.target`.
t13.hint: It is an interval timer, not a calendar one: do not use `OnCalendar`.

t14.text: Ticket: "The nightly backup has been failing silently for a few days." Write only the `Failed` lines of `~/sample/journal.txt` to `~/units/failed.txt`.

t15.text: Ticket: "The weekly report must run every Monday at 08:00, and still run after boot if the machine was off." Write `~/units/report.timer` (`OnCalendar`, the setting that catches up a missed run, `WantedBy=timers.target`).

t16.text: Count how many lines the journal sample has with `wc -l ~/sample/journal.txt`.
t16.hint: Look at the number at the start of the output.

vm.intro: On your VM (Ubuntu or Rocky/Alma) go through these in order. **Take a snapshot** first (Module 0.2). You write units under `/etc/systemd/system/`; only touch your own `backup.*` files. If something goes wrong, stop it with `sudo systemctl disable --now backup.timer`.

v01.title: Write the script and service
v01.text: First put the script in `/usr/local/bin`, then write the service file and show its content. Keep the script in `/usr/local/bin` because of SELinux.

blocks.cmd:
sudo tee /usr/local/bin/backup.sh > /dev/null <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
echo "backup done"
EOF
sudo chmod 755 /usr/local/bin/backup.sh

sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/backup.service > /dev/null <<'EOF'
[Unit]
Description=Nightly backup

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/backup.sh
EOF
cat /etc/systemd/system/backup.service

differs: If you get `Permission denied`, `sudo` is missing; `sudo` must come before `tee`.
The `EOF` line of the heredoc (`<<'EOF'`) must stand alone at the start of its line.

v02.title: Write the timer
v02.text: Write a timer that runs every night at 02:30 and catches up missed runs, then paste its content.

blocks.cmd:
sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/backup.timer > /dev/null <<'EOF'
[Unit]
Description=Run backup nightly

[Timer]
OnCalendar=*-*-* 02:30:00
Persistent=true
RandomizedDelaySec=5min

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target
EOF
cat /etc/systemd/system/backup.timer

differs: The file must be called `backup.timer`: same name as the service, different extension.
The quoted heredoc (`'EOF'`) stops the `*` from being expanded.

v03.title: Verify
v03.text: Verify the time expression and the unit files without running anything; paste the output.

blocks.expected:
Normalized form: *-*-* 02:30:00
    Next elapse: Fri 2026-11-13 02:30:00 CET
(verify: usually no output = no problem)

differs: If `verify` prints nothing, there is no problem.
On older versions the `Next elapse` text may differ slightly; the `Normalized form` line still appears.

v04.title: Install and schedule
v04.text: Run `daemon-reload`, enable the timer and see it scheduled with `list-timers`. `backup.timer` must appear in the output.

blocks.cmd:
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now backup.timer
systemctl list-timers backup.timer
blocks.expected:
NEXT                        LEFT     LAST PASSED UNIT         ACTIVATES
Fri 2026-11-13 02:30:00 CET 16h left n/a  n/a    backup.timer backup.service

differs: If you see `Unit backup.timer not found`, you skipped `daemon-reload` or the file name/path is wrong.
Because of `RandomizedDelaySec`, NEXT may be a few minutes after 02:30.

v05.title: Run by hand, read the journal
v05.text: Start the service once by hand and find the `backup done` line in its journal.

blocks.cmd:
sudo systemctl start backup.service
journalctl -u backup.service --no-pager -n 10
blocks.expected:
systemd[1]: Starting backup.service - Nightly backup...
backup.sh[1234]: backup done
systemd[1]: backup.service: Succeeded.

differs: On Rocky/RHEL the last line may read `Deactivated successfully.`; that is fine.
If you see `Failed with result 'exit-code'`, the script path or permission is wrong (`chmod 755`, `ls -Z` for SELinux).

v06.title: User timer and cleanup
v06.text: Set up a user timer without `sudo`, see it in the list; then stop it and the system timer. If no errors, press "Done".

blocks.cmd:
mkdir -p ~/.config/systemd/user
printf '[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/bin/touch %h/notes.txt
' > ~/.config/systemd/user/notes.service
printf '[Timer]
OnCalendar=hourly

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target
' > ~/.config/systemd/user/notes.timer
systemctl --user daemon-reload
systemctl --user enable --now notes.timer
systemctl --user list-timers

systemctl --user disable --now notes.timer
sudo systemctl disable --now backup.timer

differs: If you get `Failed to connect to bus`, run it in your normal login session, not via `sudo su`; `--user` needs a non-root session.
`%h` means the home directory inside a unit; the `printf` is single-quoted so the shell does not expand it.

q1.q: Which file defines **when** a job runs?
q1.explain: The timer defines 'when', the service defines 'what'; their names match.

options: Catches up a run missed while the machine was off at the next boot
Runs the job as a user instead of root
q2.explain: Persistent stores the last run time on disk; a missed run is made up at boot.

q3.q: You wrote a new `.timer` file. What must you do before `enable --now`?
q3.explain: systemd caches unit files; `daemon-reload` is required after a change.

q4.q: Where do you read a service's output and error lines?
q4.explain: systemd writes output to the journal; `-u` filters by unit.

summary: A timer is two files: `.service` defines what runs, `.timer` defines when.
`Type=oneshot` and an absolute `ExecStart` path are the standard for scheduled jobs.
`OnCalendar` is calendar time, `OnBootSec`/`OnUnitActiveSec` an interval; `Persistent=true` catches up missed runs.
Read output with `journalctl -u`; the cron line `30 2 * * *` = every day at 02:30.
User timers work without root via `~/.config/systemd/user` and `systemctl --user`.

glossary.meaning: A `.timer` unit that starts a service at a given time.
A `.service` unit that defines the command to run.
`Type=oneshot`: the command runs and finishes; suited to scheduled jobs.
`Persistent=true`: catches up a missed run at the next boot.
Adds a random start delay to avoid load spikes.
Makes systemd re-read its unit files.
The classic scheduler; `crontab` lines use five time fields.
`loginctl enable-linger`: keeps user units running while logged out.
